MARS: THE LAST LAUNCH

MARS: THE LAST LAUNCH is an interactive 3D first-person Mars exploration and space mission design game developed with Godot Engine.

Players take the role of an astronaut in a fictional Mars mission inspired by NASA's space exploration programs. They explore educational research sites based on Viking 1, InSight, and Curiosity, investigate Martian geology, collect scientific samples, and manage their limited oxygen supply.

To complete the mission, players must follow a sequence of scientific objectives, repair spacecraft systems, and design a CubeSat by selecting instruments within strict power and mass limits. Incorrect engineering decisions can lead to mission failure.

The experience concludes with CubeSat assembly and a cinematic launch sequence. By combining scientific discovery, resource management, and engineering trade-offs, the game makes the challenges of space mission design engaging and accessible.

MARS: THE LAST LAUNCH

OVERALL PROJECT GOAL

MARS: THE LAST LAUNCH is an interactive 3D first-person Mars exploration and space mission design game developed using Godot Engine.

Our goal is to help players understand how scientific objectives, limited resources, engineering decisions, and mission planning affect the success of a space mission.

Inspired by NASA's Mars exploration programs, the game combines scientific investigation, astronaut survival, spacecraft repair, CubeSat design, and a final launch sequence.

Players must do more than explore: they must make informed decisions and understand the consequences of incorrect actions.

Figure 1. The astronaut begins the mission inside the spacecraft and receives instructions before exploring Mars.

PROJECT OVERVIEW

1. Exploring the Martian Surface

Players control an astronaut from a first-person perspective. After leaving the spacecraft through an interactive airlock, they explore a simulated Martian environment.

Navigation indicators help players locate research sites, while distance measurements provide guidance during exploration.

The game features educational locations inspired by three NASA Mars missions:

Viking 1 — Basalt Investigation

The Viking 1 research site introduces players to the history of early Mars exploration. Players investigate the site and collect a basalt rock sample.

Figure 2. The Viking 1-inspired research location and basalt sample investigation.

InSight — Hematite Investigation

The InSight research site introduces scientific concepts associated with the study of Mars' interior and environmental conditions. A hematite sample is included as part of the game's fictional educational investigation.

Figure 3. The InSight-inspired research location and hematite collection activity.

Curiosity — Calcium Sulfate Investigation

The Curiosity research site focuses on Martian geology, mineral investigation, and evidence of ancient water-related processes.

Figure 4. The Curiosity-inspired research location and calcium sulfate sample investigation.

Scientific Accuracy Note: The locations are combined into a fictional, compressed educational environment. They do not represent the actual geographic distances between NASA's Mars missions. The hematite investigation draws on broader Mars geological research, including discoveries made by NASA's Opportunity rover.

2. Astronaut Survival and Oxygen Management

Exploring Mars requires careful resource management.

The astronaut's oxygen supply gradually decreases outside the spacecraft. Players must monitor their remaining oxygen and return to the spacecraft before it reaches zero.

Once safely inside, oxygen replenishes. Running out of oxygen results in mission failure.

This mechanic teaches players the importance of life-support systems and planning during extravehicular activities.

Figure 5. The astronaut monitors oxygen levels and navigation information while exploring the Martian surface.

3. Scientific Mission Objectives

Players investigate research sites, scan geological targets, collect scientific samples, and store them in an inventory.

Mission objectives must be completed in a defined sequence. Players can inspect locations freely, but attempting critical actions in the wrong order can result in mission failure.

The game provides feedback explaining unsuccessful decisions and allows players to restart their mission.

4. CubeSat Design and Engineering Constraints

An essential part of the game is the CubeSat mission-design system.

Players choose scientific instruments while respecting a simplified engineering resource budget.

Available instruments include:

  • Atmospheric Sensor
  • Surface Imaging Camera
  • Communication Module
  • Radiation Sensor

The mission has a maximum power budget of 7 units and a maximum mass budget of 7 units.

The required scientific configuration consumes 7 power units and 6 mass units. Adding the radiation sensor would exceed the available limits.

Players must evaluate the trade-offs between scientific capability and spacecraft resources.

These numerical limits are simplified educational gameplay values rather than real spacecraft engineering specifications.

Figure 6. Players select CubeSat instruments and evaluate power and mass limitations before approving their mission design.

5. Spacecraft Repair and CubeSat Assembly

After completing scientific investigations, players return to the spacecraft and complete technical objectives.

These activities include repairing spacecraft systems and assembling the CubeSat for deployment.

The sequence emphasizes the importance of completing essential engineering tasks before launch.

Figure 7. The astronaut completes engineering tasks required to prepare the CubeSat and spacecraft for the final mission stage.

6. Final Launch and Mission Success

After successfully completing the required scientific and engineering objectives, players initiate the final launch sequence.

A cinematic sequence presents the culmination of the mission.

The game also includes a mission timer and a local leaderboard that records successful completion times, encouraging players to improve their planning and decision-making.

Figure 8. The successful CubeSat launch represents the completion of the mission's scientific and engineering objectives.

EDUCATIONAL VALUE AND INNOVATION

MARS: THE LAST LAUNCH brings together several key aspects of space mission design in one interactive learning experience:

  • Scientific investigation inspired by NASA Mars missions
  • Resource management through astronaut oxygen limitations
  • Engineering trade-offs involving spacecraft power and mass
  • Mission sequencing and consequence-based decision-making
  • Spacecraft repair, CubeSat assembly, and launch preparation
  • Learning through experimentation, failure, and improvement

The project demonstrates that mission success depends not only on technological capabilities but also on careful planning, realistic constraints, and informed engineering decisions.

MARS: THE LAST LAUNCH is an independently developed educational game inspired by NASA missions and is not an official NASA mission simulator.
